newsitem.title: INDIA: India to take measures to reverse export slowdown.
newsitem.headline: India to take measures to reverse export slowdown.

text.p: An Indian government minister said on Friday that the central bank would soon unveil a plan to stimulate exports which have recently stalled, raising fears of an economic slowdown.
India's exports grew 2.38 percent in August compared to the same month in 1995. That was far below the 20.66 percent growth rate in August 1995 over the same month in 1994.
Exports in August were valued at $2.60 billion, up marginally from $2.54 billion one year earlier.
Imports fell to $2.9 billion in August, 0.7 percent lower than in the same month one year earlier.

V. Raghuraman, secretary general of the Associated Chambers of Commerce (ASSOCHAM), said on Thursday that the slowdown in export growth was "worrisome and strengthens fears of an overall economic slowdown".

Indian Commerce Minister Bolla Bulli Ramaiah said the government was in discussions with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) about exporters' complaints over a perceived shortage of liquidity to promote overseas sales.
"They (RBI) will come out with a proposal that will enable to help further the export-oriented industry," Ramaiah told Reuters on the margins of a business conference in the Indian capital.
Many Indian firms and exporters have complained that a shortage of liquidity and high interest rates have dampened industrial production and trade.
Strong growth of imports, while it can contribute to a trade imbalance, can also reflect buoyant economic demand. Export sales can add to national output.
Ramaiah said the RBI was working on "some schemes" which "will be able to come out very soon, most probably within a few days".
He said the availability of finance and reasonable interest rates were important for exports. The Commerce Ministry has discussed the availability of export finance with the RBI, Ramaiah said.
Ramaiah said he did not expect the rupee's exchange rate to be affected by the slowdown in exports. "As it is now it is stable and we hope it will continue like this," he said.
The minister said a jump in oil imports would not affect the country's foreign exchange reserves.
Oil imports in the first five months of the 1996/97 fiscal year which began in April jumped 39.3 percent to $3.7 billion against $2.7 billion in the same period last year.
"Our imports of capital goods and other things have substantially come down. Therefore the jump will not affect (reserves) that much," he said.
According to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), foreign currency reserves in September stood at $18.28 billion.
